newsitem.title: USA: US bank reform bill mostly negative - Comptroller.
newsitem.headline: US bank reform bill mostly negative - Comptroller.

text.p: The office of the Comptroller of the Currency views U.S. financial reform legislation under consideration in Congress as harmful to the banking industry and bank regulators, according to a memo obtained by Reuters on Friday.

The House Banking Committee approved the massive financial reform bill last week by a narrow 28-26 vote. The complex proposal would tear down decades-old laws separating banking from insurance and securities underwriting.
An "initial analysis" by OCC general counsel Julie Williams concluded the bill is, on balance, bad for banks.
"The negatives significantly outweigh the positives, particularly in terms of the bill's effect on the national bank charter and regulatory burdens on banks in general," Williams wrote in the memo.

"Some of these provisions will restrict the availability and raise the cost of financial services provided by banking organizations and could have a detrimental effect on (the Community Reinvestment Act)," Williams added.
The committee approved dozens of amendments before voting on the bill. Williams said several would unfairly burden banks relative to other financial service companies.
For example, the bill was amended to allow banks to own or be owned by nonfinancial, commercial companies.

But Williams noted that while the Federal Reserve would oversee all operations of a bank holding company that owned a commercial company, the central bank would have a much more limited say over a commercial company that owned a bank.
The Fed is also authorized to set different capital standards for different types of holding companies, which could result in large banks being subject to more stringent rules, Williams wrote.

A series of consumer protection amendments would apply only to banks, Williams said. Banks would have to determine if an insurance product was "appropriate" for a customer, use physically separate areas to sell uninsured products and provide inexpensive bank accounts to low-income customers.
The legislation would also roll back some powers banks currently possess, Williams wrote.
Banks would be forbidden from selling title insurance and bank subsidiaries could not be principals in certain types of insurance or certain real estate related activities.

The OCC's ability to determine what activities are permissible for national banks would also be cut back. "The deference the courts today accord OCC interpretations of the National Bank Act would be radically altered," Williams wrote.

Lawmakers and the insurance industry have criticized the OCC for expanding the authority of banks to sell insurance, but the agency has won several court challenges to its decisions. But critics managed to add provision to the bank reform bill curbing the OCC's authority in that area.

The legislation still has a long way to go before becoming law. The bill is before the House Commerce Committee, which may not vote on it until September. And companion legislation is stalled in the Senate.
A spokeswoman for the OCC declined to comment on the memo.
